Good to hear it! The product strategy happens before you write code.

I follow a simplified format from the book [shape up](https://basecamp.com/shapeup) and have for close to a decade.
[ul][li]Narrow the problem [li]Sketch out a few rough solutions to solve said problem [li]List things out of bounds \(no goes\)[li]List potential rabbit holes \(things you know could be a time bomb\) [li]Then time box it as a constraint \(less relevant - never tell the ai a time box\)

It works great for 0 -> 1 and for 1.0 to 1.1 and beyond.

I havent made videos about this ... but writing it out I realize I should

You get more leverage on your time writing code / designing if youve thought it out ahead of time.

And then you bring it into asking the AI how to further shape your idea, poke holes in it, find open questions, find where it fits into an existing codebase or where you should start if its brand new.

What HAS changed drastically is once youre in the editor...

because AI confidently paints a picture of how easy this implementation will be ...then its 4am and you're about to throw your laptop off a bridge.

So it requires having discipline around a set of steps you follow for all work.

If I spent an hour working on a new feature, I'd spend at least half that time refining the PRD. Taking that initial pitch format, doing research on tech / designs / other peoples repos I can learn from.

Then when I get to implementation, using a tool called Task Master, the majority of the intitial thinking is done. Which means the AI doesn't have to waste any valuable compute on it. Instead it plusses up and expands the idea, steel mans both sides.. and improves it.

From there you shape the idea further, actually guiding the AI to do the tasks. Making changes along the way...

And finally once you're happy with it you are now testing it locally.

A massive benefit of AI is making the 'testing' part of coding fun.

I rolled out a set of automations for my youtube videos that have 4 separate sets of tests. 4! I would've never done that without AI. Now its ready for any scale of traffic

Message me on Discord or on here and let's get your project off the ground. Need to know where you are at with it, and some other details.

Again happy to have you! Sorry for the long winded answer.

Using Typer and WP-CLI Together: A Concise Guide
Typer, a Python library for building command-line interfaces \(CLIs\), and WP-CLI, a PHP-based tool for managing WordPress sites, can be integrated to create a powerful, custom CLI for WordPress administration. This combination harnesses Python’s flexibility and WP-CLI’s robust WordPress management capabilities, using Python’s subprocess module to execute WP-CLI commands from a Typer application. The integration works by defining Typer commands that correspond to WordPress tasks. These commands trigger WP-CLI operations via subprocess, capturing and processing the output for user-friendly display or further manipulation. For instance, a Typer command to list WordPress plugins might accept the WordPress installation path as an argument, run wp plugin list --format=json through subprocess, parse the JSON response, and output plugin names and statuses.
Key Considerations for Integration
To ensure a smooth and secure setup, several factors must be addressed:

[ul][li]WP-CLI Installation: WP-CLI must be installed and available in the system’s PATH.[li]WordPress Path: Specify the WordPress directory using the --path flag or run the Typer app from within it.[li]Output Handling: WP-CLI output can be captured as plain text or JSON for structured data processing.[li]Error Handling: Implement checks for command failures or parsing errors to enhance reliability.[li]Security: Pass arguments to subprocess as a list to prevent injection vulnerabilities.
Practical Use Cases
This approach supports a variety of WordPress management tasks, such as:

[ul][li]Database Backups: Automate wp db export for regular backups.[li]Plugin Updates: Run wp plugin update --all to keep plugins current.[li]User Management: Execute wp user create to add new users efficiently. These can be bundled into a single Typer app, creating a unified CLI experience.
Advanced Features
The integration can be extended with:

[ul][li]Multi-Site Management: Use configuration files or flags to manage multiple WordPress installations.[li]Remote Execution: Integrate SSH libraries like paramiko to run WP-CLI commands on remote servers.[li]Data Analysis: Parse JSON output to analyze plugin statuses or other site metrics.
Limitations
A notable constraint is that custom WP-CLI commands cannot be written in Python; the integration relies on executing existing WP-CLI commands via subprocess.
Conclusion
By combining Typer and WP-CLI, developers can craft a tailored, Python-based CLI for WordPress management, automating tasks like backups and updates. Starting with basic commands and scaling to advanced features, this method leverages both tools’ strengths, with WP-CLI’s documentation offering further command inspiration.

I used Memory Bank for a few months before switching to Task Master.

Both Cline and Task Master rely on Cursor Rules to manage tasks behind the scenes.

Pick one system and master it.

Memory Bank is basically Cline’s version of Task Master.

Cline pioneered agentic workflows by shifting to a task-based system.
You work from `[projectBrief.md](http://projectBrief.md)` in Cline.
You work from `prd.txt` in Task Master.

Task Master improved on this by turning tasks into a table, allowing agents to work directly from the list.

This removed the need for a separate todo file that many Cline/Memory Bank users relied on.

The only time I find Memory Bank useful now is when starting a project you’re unfamiliar with.

It creates helpful files like `ProductContext`, `TechContext`, and `ActiveContext`, and Cline updates them as you work.

If I were you, I’d commit to either Task Master or Cline and get really good at it.

Swapping tools constantly kills momentum.
